extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline counsel, and attorneys involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria used in USPTO disciplinary proceedings against patent practitioners (interpretation of 37 C.F.R. professional conduct rules, burden of proof, fee-excess analysis, definitions of misconduct, and sanctioning factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority to suspend or exclude practitioners (35 U.S.C. § 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director of the USPTO may suspend or exclude a person from practice before the Patent and Trademark Office if the person is 'shown to be incompetent or disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct,' or if the person violates regulations established by the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory basis for disciplinary action; it establishes the types of conduct (incompetence, disrepute, gross misconduct, regulatory violations) that can justify exclusion or suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disreputable or gross misconduct (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not 'engage in disreputable or gross misconduct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO declined to further define the terms in the rule; courts and prior decisions (e.g., Poole) characterize 'disreputable' as unprofessional conduct violating ordinary standards of professional obligation and honor. The disciplinary rules state the minimum level of conduct below which practitioners may be disciplined (37 C.F.R. § 10.20(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not 'engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation is interpreted using common definitions: 'deceit' = behavior meant to fool; 'dishonest' = lack of honesty/trustworthiness; 'misrepresentation' includes false or misleading assertions and can include concealment or non-disclosure. Non-disclosure may have the effect of a misrepresentation (Black's; Restatement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on other conduct adversely reflecting on fitness to practice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not 'engage in any other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a catchall subsection to address other conduct that, under the totality of circumstances, shows unfitness to practice; adjudicators consider whether conduct undermines integrity, competence, or the profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on charging illegal or clearly excessive fees (37 C.F.R. § 10.36(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are prohibited from 'enter[ing] into an agreement for, charg[ing], or collect[ing] an illegal or clearly excessive fee.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 10.36 was modeled after ABA provisions. The test for 'clearly excessive' is whether 'a practitioner of ordinary prudence would be left with a definite and firm conviction that the fee is in excess of a reasonable fee.' The prohibition extends to finance charges and interest for unpaid services (case law examples cited). Whether a fee is 'legal' or 'excessive' depends on the nature of services (legal vs non-legal) and any written agreement between the parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / scope of 'legal service' under USPTO regs (37 C.F.R. § 10.1(n) and § 11.5(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Title 37 governs 'solely the practice of patent, trademark, and other law before the [USPTO].' Section 11.5(b)(1) authorizes a practitioner to perform 'those services which are reasonably necessary and incident to the preparation and prosecution of patent applications,' including preparing documents for filing, corresponding/communicating with the Office, representing a client in documents, interviews, hearings, meetings, and advising a client concerning matters pending or contemplated to be presented before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marketing and development work (e.g., product design, marketing) generally do not qualify as 'legal services' under these definitions; fees attributable to such non-legal services do not fall within §10.36's 'fees for legal services' limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in OED disciplinary proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving the alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence. Thereafter, Respondent has the burden to prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing is an intermediate standard between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt. It is used to protect particularly important liberties; quote authorities (Addington, Jimenez) describing the degree of belief required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and convincing evidence standard—definition and application
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard requires evidence 'of such weight that it produces in the mind of the trier of fact a firm belief or conviction, without hesitancy, as to the truth of the allegations.' Evidence is 'clear' if certain, unambiguous, and plain; it is 'convincing' if reasonable and persuasive enough to cause belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in both proving violations and proving affirmative defenses; tribunal must be firmly convinced of the truth of the allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory interpretation / agency deference framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Before deferring to an agency's interpretation of its regulation, the Court must determine whether the regulation's language is plain and unambiguous with regard to the dispute. If unambiguous, plain language controls; only if ambiguous may deference be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Robinson v. Shell Oil and similar authorities. This framework constrains how broadly OED interpretations of USPTO rules will be accepted in adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for whether a fee is 'per se excessive' and role of written agreements/statutory prejudice interest
rubrics_metrics.description: An interest or finance charge is not necessarily per se excessive simply because it exceeds the state's prejudgment interest statutory rate; parties may agree in writing to a higher rate. The fact that a late fee equals a high percentage of unbilled services does not automatically make it per se excessive because interest accumulates over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonableness must be assessed under the 'practitioner of ordinary prudence' test and in light of any written agreement; silence or lack of notice to client about accruing interest weighs against reasonableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of client notice and billing practices to reasonableness of fees/finance charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Charging interest or finance charges based on dates when the client was not billed and unaware that interest was accruing is unreasonable and can support findings of excessive or disreputable conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicator considers whether communications were demands for payment or merely accountings; lack of notice that interest would accrue and the timing of the first bill are significant factual considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and assessment of 'disreputable' conduct (guidance from Poole and USPTO canon)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Disreputable' conduct includes unprofessional conduct that violates ordinary standards of professional obligation and honor; the disciplinary rules set the minimum conduct level below which discipline applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicator evaluates whether practitioner conduct meets that threshold based on professional norms, prior case law, and factual context (e.g., misleading client about applicability of finance charge then imposing it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements and scope of a misrepresentation/dishonesty finding
rubrics_metrics.description: Misrepresentation includes false or misleading assertions or conduct that amounts to a false assertion; concealment or non-disclosure may be treated as misrepresentation. Dishonesty involves a lack of truthfulness, probity, or integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual facts (e.g., telling client not to worry about a fine-print finance charge and later imposing it) can transform otherwise unsavory business practices into dishonest conduct violating §10.23(b)(4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice-of-counsel defense requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish reliance on counsel as a mitigating factor, a practitioner must fully disclose all pertinent facts to counsel and in good faith rely on counsel's advice; crucially, counsel must have advised on the lawfulness of the proposed future conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance on counsel about collectability or litigation strategy is insufficient to excuse a disciplinary rule violation unless counsel specifically advised that the conduct did not violate USPTO disciplinary rules. Case law (Butler, Polytarides) cited for elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors for imposing discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sanctioning, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) existence of aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators often consult the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions to identify aggravating/mitigating factors (e.g., prior disciplinary offense is aggravating; reliance on counsel might be mitigating if all elements are met). Prior disciplinary stipulations may be treated as aggravating in later proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof requirements for retaliatory-motive/causation claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimant asserting retaliation must show a causal link between the protected activity and the adverse action; mere temporal sequence (post hoc) is insufficient to infer causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicator looks for proximate temporal proximity and other evidence of nexus; timing after a separate dispositive event (e.g., court or agency order) may undercut an inference that billing was retaliatory.
